Lecture 18

Taylor, Laurent and isolated singularities

Lecture objectives

We expand analytic functions in Taylor series on discs and Laurent series on annuli. We prove Morera’s theorem, the analyticity of locally uniform limits and of parameter integrals, and the identity theorem. We classify isolated singular points and compute residues.

Lecture 17 recovered an analytic function inside a circle from its values on the circle. In this lecture we expand the factor 1/(ζ−z)1/(\zeta-z)1/(ζ−z) of Cauchy’s formula, the Cauchy kernel, in a geometric series and obtain power series. Near a point where the function fails to be analytic the same idea gives a series with negative powers. Its coefficient of (z−z0)−1(z-z_0)^{-1}(z−z0​)−1 is the residue, which Lectures 19–21 use to evaluate integrals and sums. The lecture reads in three stages: Sections 18.1–18.3 (power series, Morera’s theorem, Taylor series), Sections 18.4–18.5 (zeros, the identity theorem, Laurent series) and Sections 18.6–18.7 (singular points, residues, parameter integrals).

18.1 Power series in the complex plane

As in Lectures 15–17, UUU is an open subset of C,\CC, Br(z0)B_r(z_0)Br​(z0​) the open disc and B‾r(z0)\overline B_r(z_0)Br​(z0​) the closed disc of radius rrr about z0,z_0z0​, and Cr(z0)C_r(z_0)Cr​(z0​) the circle about z0z_0z0​ traversed once counterclockwise. The radius of convergence of GM 30 carries over to complex power series, with the modulus in place of the absolute value.

Definition 18.1 (Power series and radius of convergence). A power series about z0∈Cz_0\in\Cz0​∈C is a series ∑n=0∞an(z−z0)n,an∈C,\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n(z-z_0)^n ,\qquad a_n\in\C ,n=0∑∞​an​(z−z0​)n,an​∈C, with (z−z0)0=1.(z-z_0)^0=1(z−z0​)0=1. Its radius of convergence is the supremum RRR of the set {ρ≥0:the sequence (∣an∣ρn) is bounded},\{\rho\ge0:\text{the sequence }(\abs{a_n}\rho^n)\text{ is bounded}\},{ρ≥0:the sequence (∣an​∣ρn) is bounded}, with R=∞R=\inftyR=∞ when the set is unbounded.

The set contains 0.00. If the sequence is bounded at ρ,\rhoρ, it is bounded at every smaller number, so the set is an interval from 000 to R.RR.

Proposition 18.2 (Convergence of a power series). Let RRR be the radius of convergence of ∑an(z−z0)n.\sum a_n(z-z_0)^n∑an​(z−z0​)n. The series converges absolutely for ∣z−z0∣<R\abs{z-z_0}<R∣z−z0​∣<R and diverges for ∣z−z0∣>R.\abs{z-z_0}>R∣z−z0​∣>R. For every rrr with 0≤r<R0\le r<R0≤r<R it converges uniformly on B‾r(z0).\overline B_r(z_0)Br​(z0​).

Proof. Let 0≤r<R.0\le r<R0≤r<R. There is a number ρ>r\rho>rρ>r for which ∣an∣ρn≤M\abs{a_n}\rho^n\le M∣an​∣ρn≤M for all n,nn, with some constant M.MM. Put q=r/ρ<1.q=r/\rho<1q=r/ρ<1. For ∣z−z0∣≤r,\abs{z-z_0}\le r∣z−z0​∣≤r, ∣an(z−z0)n∣≤∣an∣ρn(rρ)n≤Mqn.\abs{a_n(z-z_0)^n}\le\abs{a_n}\rho^n\Bigl(\frac r\rho\Bigr)^n\le Mq^n .∣an​(z−z0​)n∣≤∣an​∣ρn(ρr​)n≤Mqn. By comparison with the geometric series (GM 29) the series converges absolutely, and an absolutely convergent complex series converges (GM 31). Its tail after the index NNN satisfies ∣∑n=N+1∞an(z−z0)n∣≤∑n=N+1∞Mqn=MqN+11−q,\abs{\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty a_n(z-z_0)^n}\le\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty Mq^n=\frac{Mq^{N+1}}{1-q},​n=N+1∑∞​an​(z−z0​)n​≤n=N+1∑∞​Mqn=1−qMqN+1​, a bound independent of zzz that tends to 0.00. This is uniform convergence on B‾r(z0),\overline B_r(z_0)Br​(z0​), in the sense of GM 30 with the modulus. Every zzz with ∣z−z0∣<R\abs{z-z_0}<R∣z−z0​∣<R lies in such a closed disc.

If the series converged at a point with ∣z−z0∣>R,\abs{z-z_0}>R∣z−z0​∣>R, its terms would tend to 000 (GM 29) and so be bounded. Then ∣z−z0∣\abs{z-z_0}∣z−z0​∣ would belong to the set whose supremum is R,RR, which is impossible. ■

18.2 Morera’s theorem and locally uniform limits

In this section we deduce analyticity from vanishing integrals, and we show that analyticity survives the limits that occur in series and in integrals.

Its boundary ∂T\partial T∂T is the closed path along the segments from z1z_1z1​ to z2,z_2z2​, from z2z_2z2​ to z3z_3z3​ and from z3z_3z3​ back to z1.z_1z1​. We write [z1,z2][z_1,z_2][z1​,z2​] for the segment from z1z_1z1​ to z2z_2z2​ as a path. Recall from Lecture 15 that UUU is star-shaped about z∗∈Uz_*\in Uz∗​∈U if the segment from z∗z_*z∗​ to every point of UUU lies in U.UU.

Lemma 18.3 (Antiderivative on a star-shaped set). Let UUU be open and star-shaped about z∗,z_*z∗​, and let fff be continuous on U.UU. Suppose that ∮∂Tf(z) ⁣dz=0\oint_{\partial T}f(z)\dd z=0∮∂T​f(z)dz=0 for every closed triangle T⊂UT\subset UT⊂U that has z∗z_*z∗​ as a vertex. From here on we apply Cauchy’s theorem and Cauchy’s integral and derivative formulas to every analytic function, as Goursat’s theorem allows (Lecture 17).

Proposition 18.4 (Cauchy’s theorem on star-shaped sets). Let fff be analytic on an open set UUU that is star-shaped. Then ∮Cf(z) ⁣dz=0\oint_Cf(z)\dd z=0∮C​f(z)dz=0 for every closed path CCC in U.UU.

Proof. By Goursat’s theorem (Lecture 17) the integral of fff around every closed triangle in UUU vanishes. Lemma 18.3 gives an antiderivative of fff on U,UU, and the proposition on the integral of a derivative in Lecture 17 gives ∮Cf ⁣dz=0.\oint_Cf\dd z=0∮C​fdz=0. ■

Discs, half-planes, the whole plane and the cut plane C∖(−∞,0]\C\setminus(-\infty,0]C∖(−∞,0] are star-shaped (Lecture 15). The punctured plane is not star-shaped, and on it the analytic function 1/z1/z1/z has ∮C1(0) ⁣dz/z=2πi.\oint_{C_1(0)}\dd z/z=2\pi\iu∮C1​(0)​dz/z=2πi.

Theorem 18.5 (Morera’s theorem). Let fff be continuous on an open set U,UU, and let ∮∂Tf(z) ⁣dz=0\oint_{\partial T}f(z)\dd z=0∮∂T​f(z)dz=0 for every closed triangle T⊂U.T\subset UT⊂U. Then fff is analytic on U.UU.

Proof. Fix z0∈Uz_0\in Uz0​∈U and a disc Br(z0)⊂U.B_r(z_0)\subset UBr​(z0​)⊂U. The disc is star-shaped about z0,z_0z0​, so Lemma 18.3 gives a function FFF on Br(z0)B_r(z_0)Br​(z0​) with F′=f.F'=fF′=f. This derivative is continuous. By Cauchy’s integral formula for functions with a continuous derivative (Lecture 17), FFF satisfies Cauchy’s formula on every closed disc inside Br(z0).B_r(z_0)Br​(z0​). By Cauchy’s derivative formulas (Lecture 17), FFF has complex derivatives of every order there. In particular f=F′f=F'f=F′ is complex differentiable on Br(z0).B_r(z_0)Br​(z0​). Since z0z_0z0​ was arbitrary, fff is analytic on U.UU. ■

Definition 18.6 (Locally uniform convergence). Functions fnf_nfn​ on UUU converge locally uniformly to fff on UUU if every point z0∈Uz_0\in Uz0​∈U has a disc Br(z0)⊂UB_r(z_0)\subset UBr​(z0​)⊂U on which fn→ff_n\to ffn​→f uniformly, that is, sup⁡z∈Br(z0)∣fn(z)−f(z)∣→0\sup_{z\in B_r(z_0)}\abs{f_n(z)-f(z)}\to0supz∈Br​(z0​)​∣fn​(z)−f(z)∣→0 as n→∞.n\to\inftyn→∞.

Let gng_ngn​ and ggg be continuous on the image of a path CCC and let gn→gg_n\to ggn​→g uniformly there. The length estimate gives ∣∫Cgn ⁣dz−∫Cg ⁣dz∣≤sup⁡C∣gn−g∣ L(C)⟶0.\abs{\int_Cg_n\dd z-\int_Cg\dd z}\le\sup_C\abs{g_n-g}\,L(C)\longrightarrow0 .​∫C​gn​dz−∫C​gdz​≤Csup​∣gn​−g∣L(C)⟶0.(18.1) Applied to partial sums, this permits termwise integration of a series that converges uniformly on the image of C.CC.

18.3 Taylor series

We now prove that an analytic function is the sum of a convergent power series near each point, as Lecture 15 announced, by expanding 1/(ζ−z)1/(\zeta-z)1/(ζ−z) in Cauchy’s formula as a geometric series.

Theorem 18.9 (Taylor’s theorem). Let fff be analytic on a disc BR(z0),B_R(z_0)BR​(z0​), where 0<R≤∞0<R\le\infty0<R≤∞ and B∞(z0)=C.B_\infty(z_0)=\CB∞​(z0​)=C. Then f(z)=∑n=0∞an(z−z0)n(z∈BR(z0)),f(z)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n(z-z_0)^n\qquad(z\in B_R(z_0)),f(z)=n=0∑∞​an​(z−z0​)n(z∈BR​(z0​)),(18.3) and for every rrr with 0<r<R0<r<R0<r<R an=f(n)(z0)n!=12πi∮Cr(z0)f(ζ)(ζ−z0)n+1 ⁣dζ.a_n=\frac{f^{(n)}(z_0)}{n!}=\frac1{2\pi\iu}\oint_{C_r(z_0)}\frac{f(\zeta)}{(\zeta-z_0)^{n+1}}\dd\zeta .an​=n!f(n)(z0​)​=2πi1​∮Cr​(z0​)​(ζ−z0​)n+1f(ζ)​dζ.(18.4) In particular, the radius of convergence of the series is at least R.RR.

Proof. Fix z∈BR(z0)z\in B_R(z_0)z∈BR​(z0​) and choose rrr with ∣z−z0∣<r<R.\abs{z-z_0}<r<R∣z−z0​∣<r<R. Let C=Cr(z0)C=C_r(z_0)C=Cr​(z0​) and q=∣z−z0∣/r<1.q=\abs{z-z_0}/r<1q=∣z−z0​∣/r<1. For ζ\zetaζ on C,CC, 1ζ−z=1(ζ−z0)(1−z−z0ζ−z0)=∑n=0∞(z−z0)n(ζ−z0)n+1,\frac1{\zeta-z}=\frac1{(\zeta-z_0)\bigl(1-\frac{z-z_0}{\zeta-z_0}\bigr)} =\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{(z-z_0)^n}{(\zeta-z_0)^{n+1}},ζ−z1​=(ζ−z0​)(1−ζ−z0​z−z0​​)1​=n=0∑∞​(ζ−z0​)n+1(z−z0​)n​, a geometric series whose terms have modulus qn/r.q^n/rqn/r. By the tail bound in the proof of Proposition 18.2, it converges uniformly in ζ\zetaζ on C.CC. Multiplied by f(ζ),f(\zeta)f(ζ), which is bounded on C,CC, it still converges uniformly. Cauchy’s formula and termwise integration (18.1) give f(z)=12πi∮Cf(ζ)ζ−z ⁣dζ=∑n=0∞(12πi∮Cf(ζ)(ζ−z0)n+1 ⁣dζ)(z−z0)n.f(z)=\frac1{2\pi\iu}\oint_C\frac{f(\zeta)}{\zeta-z}\dd\zeta =\sum_{n=0}^\infty\Bigl(\frac1{2\pi\iu}\oint_C\frac{f(\zeta)}{(\zeta-z_0)^{n+1}}\dd\zeta\Bigr)(z-z_0)^n .f(z)=2πi1​∮C​ζ−zf(ζ)​dζ=n=0∑∞​(2πi1​∮C​(ζ−z0​)n+1f(ζ)​dζ)(z−z0​)n. Its radius of convergence is 1,11, since its terms have modulus ∣z∣2n.\abs z^{2n}∣z∣2n. On the real line nothing happens at x=±1.x=\pm1x=±1. In the plane, 1/(1+z2)1/(1+z^2)1/(1+z2) is unbounded near ±i,\pm\iu±i, at the distance 111 from 0.00. The radius of the real series is set by the complex points where the function is not analytic. ◃

18.4 Zeros and the identity theorem

A power series shows how an analytic function vanishes.

Definition 18.11 (Zero of order m).mm). Let fff be analytic at z0z_0z0​ with f(z0)=0,f(z_0)=0f(z0​)=0, and suppose that some derivative f(n)(z0)f^{(n)}(z_0)f(n)(z0​) is nonzero. Let m≥1m\ge1m≥1 be the smallest such n.nn. Then z0z_0z0​ is a zero of order mmm of f.ff. A zero of order 111 is simple.

18.6 Isolated singular points

We now consider singular points (Lecture 17) about which fff is analytic on a punctured disc.

Definition 18.19 (Isolated singular point). Let fff be analytic on a punctured disc Br(z0)∖{z0},B_r(z_0)\setminus\{z_0\}Br​(z0​)∖{z0​}, with the Laurent series ∑n∈Zan(z−z0)n\sum_{n\in\Z}a_n(z-z_0)^n∑n∈Z​an​(z−z0​)n there. If fff is not analytic at z0,z_0z0​, in particular if fff is not defined at z0,z_0z0​, the point z0z_0z0​ is an isolated singular point (an isolated singularity) of f.ff. Such a point is

  • a removable singularity of fff if a−n=0a_{-n}=0a−n​=0 for every n≥1;n\ge1n≥1;

  • a pole of order mmm of fff if a−m≠0a_{-m}\ne0a−m​=0 and a−n=0a_{-n}=0a−n​=0 for every n>m;n>mn>m; a pole of order 111 is a simple pole;

  • an essential singularity of fff if a−n≠0a_{-n}\ne0a−n​=0 for infinitely many n≥1.n\ge1n≥1.

The three cases exclude each other and cover every possibility. They depend only on the values of fff off z0.z_0z0​. At a removable singularity the Laurent series is a power series, so the value a0a_0a0​ at z0z_0z0​ makes fff analytic on the whole disc (Proposition 18.8). The point 000 is a simple pole of 1/z,1/z1/z, as announced in Lecture 16.

Summary

Expanding the Cauchy kernel in geometric series turns Cauchy’s formula into a power series on a disc and a Laurent series on an annulus. Vanishing triangle integrals (Morera) pass to locally uniform limits and to dominated parameter integrals.

  • Series: f(z)=∑n∈Zan(z−z0)nf(z)=\sum_{n\in\Z}a_n(z-z_0)^nf(z)=∑n∈Z​an​(z−z0​)n on every annulus r1<∣z−z0∣<r2r_1<\abs{z-z_0}<r_2r1​<∣z−z0​∣<r2​ on which fff is analytic, with the coefficients (18.7); on a disc (r1=0,r_1=0r1​=0, fff analytic at z0)z_0z0​) this is the Taylor series; the expansion depends on the set.

  • Analyticity tests: vanishing triangle integrals of a continuous function (Morera); locally uniform limits of analytic functions; ∫JF(z,t) ⁣dt\int_JF(z,t)\dd t∫J​F(z,t)dt with FFF analytic in z,zz, continuous, and locally dominated by an integrable g(t).g(t)g(t).

  • Identity theorem: on a domain, an analytic function whose zeros have a limit point in the domain vanishes.

  • Isolated singular points and residues: removable (bounded nearby), pole of order mmm (f=(z−z0)−mg,f=(z-z_0)^{-m}gf=(z−z0​)−mg, g(z0)≠0),g(z_0)\ne0g(z0​)=0), essential (infinitely many negative powers; e1/z\ee^{1/z}e1/z at 0);00); Res⁡z=z0f=a−1,\Res_{z=z_0}f=a_{-1}Resz=z0​​f=a−1​, with Res⁡z=z0g/h=g(z0)/h′(z0)\Res_{z=z_0}g/h=g(z_0)/h'(z_0)Resz=z0​​g/h=g(z0​)/h′(z0​) when h(z0)=0≠h′(z0).h(z_0)=0\ne h'(z_0)h(z0​)=0=h′(z0​).

Lecture 19 adds the residues inside a closed path to evaluate contour integrals and, through them, real integrals.

Self-check

4 questions. Answer without looking back at the notes; a first miss gives a hint and a second try. Enter numbers with a decimal point.

1. What are the first two nonzero terms in the Laurent expansion of 1/[z(1−z)]1/[z(1-z)]1/[z(1−z)] about zero for ∣z∣>1\abs z>1∣z∣>1, ordered by decreasing power of zzz?

Hint. Write the geometric series using a ratio whose modulus is less than one on the specified annulus.

Factor the function as −z−2(1−z−1)−1-z^{-2}(1-z^{-1})^{-1}−z−2(1−z−1)−1. The geometric series in z−1z^{-1}z−1 starts with 1+z−11+z^{-1}1+z−1, so the two terms are −z−2−z−3-z^{-2}-z^{-3}−z−2−z−3. The terms z−1+1z^{-1}+1z−1+1 use the series for ∣z∣<1\abs z<1∣z∣<1. Two plus signs lose the prefactor’s minus sign. Alternating signs would require the opposite geometric ratio.

2. The function f(z)=sin⁡(π/z)f(z)=\sin(\pi/z)f(z)=sin(π/z) is analytic on 0<∣z∣<20<\abs z<20<∣z∣<2 and vanishes at z=1/nz=1/nz=1/n for positive integers nnn. Why does the identity theorem fail to imply f≡0f\equiv0f≡0 on this domain?

Hint. Locate the limit of the zero sequence and check whether the function is defined there.

The sequence tends to zero, which is excluded from the domain. The identity theorem requires a limit point of the zeros inside the domain. The punctured disc is connected, and a real sequence can supply the required limit point if its limit is inside. Analyticity on the whole plane is unnecessary.

3. Find Res⁡z=0(e2z/z3)\Res_{z=0}\bigl(\ee^{2z}/z^3\bigr)Resz=0​(e2z/z3). Round to two decimal places.

Enter a valid number using a decimal point.

Hint. Which Taylor coefficient of the numerator becomes the coefficient of z−1z^{-1}z−1?

The numerator is nonzero at zero, so the pole has order three. The term of e2z\ee^{2z}e2z with z2z^2z2, divided by z3z^3z3, gives the term with z−1z^{-1}z−1. Its coefficient is 22/2!=22^2/2!=222/2!=2.

4. For F(z)=∫0∞e−ztsin⁡t ⁣dtF(z)=\int_0^\infty\ee^{-zt}\sin t\dd tF(z)=∫0∞​e−ztsintdt, which is an integrable bound on the modulus of the integrand, uniform over ∣z−1∣≤1/2\abs{z-1}\le1/2∣z−1∣≤1/2?

Hint. Find the smallest possible real part of zzz in the disc.

On the disc, Re⁡z≥1/2\Re z\ge1/2Rez≥1/2 and ∣sin⁡t∣≤1\abs{\sin t}\le1∣sint∣≤1, so the modulus is bounded by e−t/2\ee^{-t/2}e−t/2, which is integrable. At z=1/2z=1/2z=1/2 and t=π/2t=\pi/2t=π/2 the bound is attained, so both faster exponentials fail there. The constant bounds the integrand but is not integrable over the half-line.
